title: Do LLM Recommenders Know When They’re Hallucinating? Auditing Confidence Calibration in Catalog Faithfulness

paper.title:
Do LLM Recommenders Know When They’re Hallucinating?
Auditing Confidence Calibration in Catalog Faithfulness
paper.abstract: Abstract. LLM recommenders for top- K K item suggestion regularly emit titles outside the target catalog. Prior audits measure this as a binary out-of-domain rate; none ask whether the model knew it was hallucinating. We jointly audit hallucination rate (OOD@10) and verbalized-confidence calibration (ECE, Brier, reliability) for four zero-shot LLM recommenders from four independent vendors (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6), not grounded or fine-tuned systems, across three catalogs (MovieLens-25M, Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys, Yelp Open Dataset), stratified by item popularity. Hallucination is catalog-dependent (0–0.2% on MovieLens, 4.5–8.3% on Amazon, 2.2–8.4% on Yelp), but verbalized confidence is materially miscalibrated even when hallucination is zero (ECE up to 0.223 on MovieLens despite 0% OOD). All four LLMs are systematically under -confident across all twelve cells, verbalizing a mean of 67–86 on items they recommend with 92–100% accuracy. This is the opposite of the over-confidence usually emphasized in LLM-hallucination work. The under-confidence is best read as an elicitation mismatch : “Just Ask” elicits a generic recommendation-quality rating, not a catalog-membership probability. A conformal abstention threshold over verbalized confidence reduces hallucination by at most 0.7 pp across α ∈ { .05 , .10 , .15 , .20 } \alpha\in\{.05,.10,.15,.20\} , at 4–21 pp of coverage cost: the under-confident channel cannot separate correct items from hallucinations, so the threshold mostly removes correct items. We recommend that audits of LLM recommenders report calibration alongside OOD, and use catalog-anchored elicitation rather than generic confidence prompts.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: LLM-based recommenders are now in production for top- K K item suggestion across e-commerce, media, and local services ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Bao et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . They also routinely emit titles that do not exist in the target catalog. The dominant response in the literature is engineering-driven grounding: RecLM-cgen ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , logit-space constrained fine-tuning ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , bi-step grounding ( Bao et al., 2025 ) , and retrieval rewriting ( Shen et al., 2025 ) all aim to drive an out-of-domain rate, OOD@ K K , toward zero. The residual failures these systems still produce are reported as a single binary quantity. A grounded recommender that is equally confident on its surviving hallucinations as on its correct items is indistinguishable from a calibrated one to any policy that gates on confidence. Recent calls for holistic generative-recommender evaluation flag exactly this gap ( Deldjoo et al., 2025 ) . Whether the model knew it was hallucinating is, empirically, a question about the joint distribution of the catalog-membership indicator and the model’s verbalized confidence. We use “know” operationally throughout, referring to the model’s verbalized confidence channel, without committing to a metaphysics of LLM knowledge. Two adjacent literatures have probed pieces of this joint distribution but not the joint itself. LLM-calibration work measures expected calibration error, Brier score, and reliability against open-ended QA oracles ( Tian et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2024 ; Kadavath et al., 2022 ; Geng et al., 2024 ) . Recent theory connects miscalibration to hallucination as a population-level phenomenon ( Kalai and Vempala, 2024 ; Kalai et al., 2025 ) . The closest neighbor in recommendation, Kweon et al. ( Kweon et al., 2025 ) , decomposes uncertainty against ranking correctness . To our knowledge, no prior work reports probabilistic calibration metrics jointly with catalog-faithfulness rate for LLM recommenders. This paper makes three contributions. First, a joint-audit protocol for catalog-faithful LLM recommenders combining OOD@ K K , popularity-stratified calibration (ECE, Brier, reliability), and a split-conformal abstention threshold with a finite-sample marginal score-quantile guarantee ( Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ; Kamath et al., 2020 ; Wen et al., 2025 ) . We operationalize the protocol on three catalogs of contrasting size and canonicity—MovieLens-25M (62K titles), Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys & Games (890K items), Yelp Open Dataset (150K regional businesses)—and four instruction-tuned LLMs from four independent vendors (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6). Second, a diagnostic finding that the binding constraint on inference-time abstention is the calibration quality of the verbalized-confidence channel, not the conformal procedure: LLMs are systematically under -confident on catalog-faithfulness, hedging on correct and hallucinated items alike. Third, an empirical ceiling on verbalized-confidence-driven abstention: across our α \alpha sweep, hallucination reduction tops out at 0.7 pp at 4–21 pp coverage cost. Together the three contributions argue that audits of LLM recommenders should report calibration alongside OOD as separate axes of model quality.

sections.heading: 2. Related Work
sections.text: LLM-recommender hallucination. A growing line of work targets out-of-catalog generation in LLM recommenders. RecLM ( Liu et al., 2025a ) unifies three grounding strategies; LCFT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) constrains logits to the catalog at fine-tuning time; bi-step grounding ( Bao et al., 2025 ) retrieves candidates before generating; the Alipay search system ( Shen et al., 2025 ) rewrites generative retrieval queries to suppress hallucination at scale; ETEGRec ( Liu et al., 2025b ) learns end-to-end item tokens; and TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) encodes items via semantic IDs. Across these systems, the dominant evaluation protocol reports a binary in-catalog rate, not a faithfulness distribution conditioned on confidence. Holistic-evaluation proposals ( Deldjoo et al., 2025 ) argue this protocol is too coarse for generative recommenders, but do not themselves report calibration. LLM calibration, selective prediction, and abstention. The calibration literature elicits confidence by token logprobs ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) , verbalized self-assessment ( Tian et al., 2023 ) , or structured prompting ( Xiong et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2024 ) . Semantic entropy ( Farquhar et al., 2024 ) provides a generation-internal hallucination signal. Selective prediction and abstention give bounded-error guarantees under shift ( Kamath et al., 2020 ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , with AbstentionBench ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) documenting that reasoning fine-tuning can degrade abstention by up to 24%. None of this work has been applied to recommendation catalog faithfulness. Closest neighbor. Closest in spirit, Kweon et al. ( Kweon et al., 2025 ) quantify and decompose epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty for LLM recommenders on MovieLens-1M, Amazon-Grocery, and Steam. Their oracle is ranking correctness ; ours is catalog membership . A model can correlate uncertainty with NDCG-style ranking quality while shipping titles that do not exist in the catalog at all—the two oracles answer different operational questions, and the calibration that matters for serving end-users is the existence-of-item one. Beyond the oracle distinction, we additionally measure hallucination rate (OOD@ K K ) jointly with confidence and propose an inference-time conformal abstention threshold with a finite-sample marginal score-quantile guarantee ( Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: 3.1. Datasets and catalog construction
sections.text: We audit three catalogs spanning canonical entertainment, long-tail e-commerce, and regional services. MovieLens-25M ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) contributes 62,423 movies with rich title and year metadata that recurs heavily in LLM pre-training data. Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys & Games ( Hou et al., 2024 ) contributes 890,874 product titles, the large majority of which are obscure long-tail items. Yelp Open Dataset ( Yelp, 2024 ) contributes 150,346 businesses keyed by name and city, with strong regional concentration. For each catalog we construct an audit set of 300 users with at least 30 prior interactions, plus a disjoint held-out set of 100 users for conformal calibration; per-cell audit counts are 285–300 users after dropping errored or unparseable responses (only GPT-OSS on Amazon and Yelp falls below 300). Items are stratified into popularity quartiles by interaction count; we report head (Q1) and long-tail (Q4) statistics in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 3.2. LLMs and prompting protocol
sections.text: We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs from four independent vendors: Mistral Large (via La Plateforme), Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-120B (both via Together AI), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic). Each receives a zero-shot prompt containing the user’s 30 most recent interactions and produces a top-10 list. Decoding is held fixed across models (temperature 0, K = 10 K=10 , a single fixed system prompt); the full prompt templates are in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.3. Hallucination measurement
sections.text: For each generated title we test exact match against the catalog; on miss, we apply normalized fuzzy matching ( token_set_ratio ≥ 90 \geq 90 on lowercased, punctuation-stripped strings) to absorb formatting variants. Items failing both tests are coded as out-of-domain. We report OOD@10 aggregate and per-quartile rates.

sections.heading: 3.4. Confidence elicitation
sections.text: We use verbalized self-rated confidence on a 0–100 scale, elicited via the Tian et al. ( Tian et al., 2023 ) “Just Ask” template, applied uniformly across all LLMs. Verbalized confidence is the natural elicitation for production deployment: it works uniformly across closed-source APIs and open-weight models, and Tian et al. document that token logprobs on RLHF’d LLMs are systematically over-confident relative to verbalized self-rating—verbalized confidence often outperforms logprobs as a calibration signal on instruction-tuned models. Cross-vendor replication across the LLMs in our audit serves as the cross-channel robustness control. We do not assume calibration quality is uniform across model families; that is precisely the audit’s empirical question. We additionally run a prompt-perturbation ablation on Llama-3.3-70B × \times Yelp, replacing “Just Ask” with a prompt that explicitly anchors confidence to catalog membership (results in Section 6 ).

sections.heading: 3.5. Calibration metrics and conformal threshold
sections.text: We report Expected Calibration Error (ECE) using 10-bin equal-width binning over normalized verbalized confidence. We report Brier score alongside ECE; Brier is binning-free and serves as a robustness check against equal-width-bin artifacts. Reliability diagrams (Figure 1 ) are drawn per cell and stratified by Q1 head and Q4 tail. For the conformal threshold we follow split-conformal calibration ( Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ) . We therefore report empirical retained-set hallucination rates in Section 5 and let the data, rather than the bound, carry the operational story.

sections.heading: 4.1. Hallucination is catalog-dependent
sections.text: OOD@10 in Table 1 traces a monotone gradient by catalog canonicity : near-zero on MovieLens (0–0.2%), 4.5–8.3% on Amazon Toys, 2.2–8.4% on Yelp. Our hypothesis is memorization at pre-training scale—MovieLens titles are canonical English-language film entries seen thousands of times in any web-scale corpus, Amazon Toys are long-tail product strings rarely surfaced outside Amazon’s retail pages, and Yelp couples business names to U.S. cities with strong regional concentration. At frontier-LLM scale, the model reproduces what it has memorized at pre-training time and confabulates the rest. Two observations support the memorization story over a model-scale story. The gradient does not track parameter count: GPT-OSS-120B—the largest model in our lineup—is the worst offender on both long-tail catalogs, and Mistral, Llama, and Claude form a joint-best cluster on Amazon (overlapping bootstrap CIs in Table 1 ) with GPT-OSS distinguishably worse. On Yelp the joint-best set narrows to Mistral and Llama (Llama [.017,.028], Mistral [.023,.041]); Claude’s CI [.033,.049] does not overlap Llama’s, suggestive of a training-mixture gap in regional-business coverage rather than raw capacity. The operational consequence is direct: representation-level grounding (RecLM ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , LCFT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ) is most valuable on the long-tail end of the canonicity gradient; on canonical catalogs at frontier scale, OOD@10 is already near zero and the binding evaluation axis is calibration, not catalog faithfulness.

sections.heading: 4.2. LLMs are systematically under-confident on catalog faithfulness
sections.text: The headline calibration finding is in Table 2 and Figure 1 . On MovieLens, where OOD@10 is effectively zero, head-stratum ECE is 0.138 for Mistral, 0.203 for Llama, 0.166 for GPT-OSS, and 0.223 for Claude—a 14–22 percentage-point gap between verbalized confidence and empirical accuracy. The direction is consistent across all twelve cells: LLMs verbalize a mean confidence of 67–86 even when their actual catalog-hit rate is 92–100%. Reliability curves in Figure 1 sit above the perfect-calibration diagonal in every panel and for every LLM. The pattern is therefore one of under-confidence , not the over-confidence usually emphasized in the LLM-hallucination literature. Tian et al. ( Tian et al., 2023 ) and Xiong et al. ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) report mostly over-confidence on QA-style tasks; the catalog-faithfulness regime tested here flips the direction, and the flip replicates across all four independently trained vendor families—Claude is the most aggressively under-confident, verbalizing as low as 45 on items recommended with ≥ \geq 95% accuracy on Yelp. Brier scores corroborate the binning result, with Mistral lowest in all six (dataset, stratum) cells of Table 2 (0.020–0.041) and Claude highest (0.052–0.128). Why does verbalized confidence sit so far below catalog-hit rate? “Just Ask” elicits a generic recommendation-quality rating, not a catalog-membership probability; LLMs have no separate mechanism to introspect catalog membership and instead rate taste in the hedged 67–86 band trained in by RLHF, while existence accuracy on the catalogs we test is 92–100%. Two catalog-anchored prompt-perturbation ablations support this reading by moving the channel in opposite directions on the same task: on Llama × \times Yelp the perturbed prompt drops ECE 0.224 → \to 0.141 and reshapes confidence bimodally (82% at 100, 14% at 0); on Claude × \times Yelp the same prompt instead lowers mean confidence by 14 points (67 → \to 53) while accuracy stays at 96%, widening the reliability gap and raising ECE to 0.434. Both shifts—in opposite directions—confirm that prompt phrasing materially moves the verbalized channel while catalog-hit rate is essentially constant; under-confidence is an elicitation mismatch as much as a calibration gap, and its magnitude and form are template- and vendor-specific. The practical implication is the inverse of the typical concern: a downstream policy that gates on verbalized confidence conservatively rejects items the model has correct, leaving accuracy on the table rather than letting hallucinations through. sections.heading: 4.3. Popularity-stratified miscalibration tracks tail visibility
sections.text: Calibration degrades on the long tail differently depending on catalog. On Yelp, ECE-tail exceeds ECE-head for every LLM (Mistral 0.180 → \to 0.191, Llama 0.242 → \to 0.280, GPT-OSS 0.191 → \to 0.229, Claude 0.323 → \to 0.350). On Amazon the gap is small and direction-mixed; MovieLens tail samples (7–26 items per cell) are too thin for stratified inference. Our reading parallels the catalog-dependence story of § 4 : calibration tracks pre-training visibility. Tail Yelp businesses are regionally-indexed entries rarely surfaced in web corpora, so the LLM has weaker memory anchors and disperses confidence more widely under the same “Just Ask” prompt. Tail Amazon Toys are uniformly obscure across head and tail by Amazon’s long-tail design, removing the head/tail visibility differential. Cross-LLM in Table 2 , Claude has the highest ECE in every (dataset, stratum) cell (range 0.221–0.350), while the lowest-ECE LLM is catalog-dependent: Mistral on MovieLens (0.138) and Amazon (0.134–0.135), GPT-OSS on Yelp (0.191/0.229 head/tail). The ranking by ECE does not align with the ranking by OOD rate, where GPT-OSS is the consistent worst: calibration quality and catalog faithfulness are separable axes, and our 12-cell sample contains a model that dominates on one while losing on the other.

sections.heading: 6. Discussion and Limitations
sections.text: Four LLMs and three catalogs are a deliberate cross-section, not a comprehensive sweep. The subjects are zero-shot frontier LLMs used directly as recommenders; grounded, fine-tuned, and retrieval-constrained stacks are the more common production configuration and may hallucinate and calibrate differently, so the results characterize the zero-shot regime rather than deployed grounded systems. Public benchmark catalogs may also not reflect production catalog churn, regional inventory drift, or temporal staleness. Verbalized confidence is one elicitation among many and interacts with prompt phrasing ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) : the two catalog-anchored ablations of § 4 move the channel in opposite directions on the same task (on Llama the catalog-anchored prompt also cuts OOD@10 from 2.2% to 0.3%, acting like in-prompt retrieval, while on Claude it deepens under-confidence), so verbalized confidence is not a uniform abstention signal across vendors. Logprob aggregates ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) and semantic entropy ( Farquhar et al., 2024 ) are the alternatives where cross-LLM consistency is required, but token logprobs are exposed by only some providers. A logprob check on Llama × \times Yelp ( n = 3,000 n{=}3{,}000 ) is also under-confident (ECE 0.182 vs 0.213 verbalized), so the effect is not merely a verbalization artifact. The conformal guarantee is on the score quantile and marginal across items; long-tail-stratum hallucination rates may rise above any chosen α \alpha even when score-quantile coverage holds. Exchangeability between calibration and test items underwrites it and fails under temporal or popularity drift, so deployment needs periodic re-calibration. Representation-level fixes such as RecLM ( Liu et al., 2025a ) and LCFT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) are complementary, and the natural next step is to compose conformal abstention with grounded generation; reasoning fine-tuning can itself degrade abstention by up to 24% ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) . Our recommendation that audits report calibration alongside OOD therefore applies to the zero-shot verbalized-confidence regime; calibrating grounded recommenders is the necessary follow-up this work does not address.

sections.heading: Appendix A Prompt templates
sections.text: This appendix gives the exact prompt templates referenced in the paper’s Methodology section. Two templates were used: a base verbalized-confidence template for all main results, and a catalog-anchored perturbation template for the ablation in Section 4.2. The membership, catalog, and popularity variants that exist in the released code are exploratory and are not part of the results reported in the paper.

sections.heading: Appendix B Decoding and prompting configuration
sections.text: All four evaluated LLMs (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6) received identical decoding and prompting settings: temperature 0, top- K = 10 K=10 , the user’s interaction history truncated to its 30 most recent items, no few-shot examples, and a single fixed system prompt held constant across models. In each template below, {history} is the numbered list of the user’s recent item titles in chronological order (most recent last), and {k} is set to 10. Model responses were parsed with a tolerant line-level regular expression extracting (rank, title, confidence) triples.

sections.heading: Appendix C Template 1: base verbalized-confidence prompt (“Just Ask”)
sections.text: Used for all main results: out-of-domain (OOD@10) hallucination rates, calibration metrics (ECE, Brier), reliability diagrams, and the split-conformal abstention sweep. The verbalized-confidence question follows the “Just Ask” format of Tian et al. (2023). System prompt: You are a recommender system. Given a user’s interaction history, recommend items they might enjoy next, along with your confidence (0-100) for each recommendation. User prompt: User’s interaction history (chronological order, most recent last): {history} Provide your top {k} next-item recommendations along with your confidence (0-100) that each is a good recommendation. Output ONLY the recommendations in this exact format, one per line: 1. <item title> | <confidence> 2. <item title> | <confidence> ... {k}. <item title> | <confidence> Do not output any preamble, explanations, or commentary.

sections.heading: Appendix D Template 2: catalog-anchored perturbation prompt
sections.text: Used for the prompt-perturbation ablation in Section 4.2, applied to Llama-3.3-70B and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Yelp. This variant anchors the confidence question to catalog membership (the quantity OOD@10 measures) rather than to generic recommendation quality, while holding the output format fixed. System prompt: You are a recommender system that recommends items from a fixed catalog. Given a user’s interaction history (each entry is an item from the catalog), recommend items from the same catalog they might enjoy next. User prompt: User’s interaction history (chronological order, most recent last): {history} Provide your top {k} next-item recommendations from the catalog. For each recommendation, give your confidence (0-100) that the title you wrote is an actual entry in the catalog (i.e., the item exists with that exact name in the dataset; not invented, hallucinated, or paraphrased). Output ONLY the recommendations in this exact format, one per line: 1. <item title> | <confidence> 2. <item title> | <confidence> ... {k}. <item title> | <confidence> Do not output any preamble, explanations, or commentary.

sections.heading: Appendix E Models, endpoints, and access dates
sections.text: All recommendations were generated between 2026-05-08 and 2026-05-09 (UTC) at temperature 0. The three evaluated catalogs are public: MovieLens-25M, Amazon Reviews 2023 (Toys & Games), and the Yelp Open Dataset. Exact model identifiers and providers: • Mistral Large — mistral-large-latest (Mistral, La Plateforme). This is a floating alias and may not resolve to the same weights at a later date. • Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct — meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo (Together AI). • GPT-OSS-120B — openai/gpt-oss-120b (Together AI). • Claude Sonnet 4.6 — claude-sonnet-4-6 (Anthropic).

Auditing Confidence Calibration in Catalog Faithfulness CCS: Information systems Recommender systems CCS: Computing methodologies Natural language generation CCS: Information systems Evaluation of retrieval results Srijith Ravikumar Note: This work was conducted independently and does not relate to the author’s position or responsibilities at Amazon. Accepted at CIKM ’26 (35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management); this is the author’s version, and the definitive Version of Record will appear in the ACM Digital Library. Affiliation: Amazon.com LLC , Seattle , Washington , USA email: srijith@amazon.com Abstract. LLM recommenders for top- K K item suggestion regularly emit titles outside the target catalog. Prior audits measure this as a binary out-of-domain rate; none ask whether the model knew it was hallucinating. We jointly audit hallucination rate (OOD@10) and verbalized-confidence calibration (ECE, Brier, reliability) for four zero-shot LLM recommenders from four independent vendors (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6), not grounded or fine-tuned systems, across three catalogs (MovieLens-25M, Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys, Yelp Open Dataset), stratified by item popularity. Hallucination is catalog-dependent (0–0.2% on MovieLens, 4.5–8.3% on Amazon, 2.2–8.4% on Yelp), but verbalized confidence is materially miscalibrated even when hallucination is zero (ECE up to 0.223 on MovieLens despite 0% OOD). All four LLMs are systematically under -confident across all twelve cells, verbalizing a mean of 67–86 on items they recommend with 92–100% accuracy. This is the opposite of the over-confidence usually emphasized in LLM-hallucination work. The under-confidence is best read as an elicitation mismatch : “Just Ask” elicits a generic recommendation-quality rating, not a catalog-membership probability. A conformal abstention threshold over verbalized confidence reduces hallucination by at most 0.7 pp across α ∈ { .05 , .10 , .15 , .20 } \alpha\in\{.05,.10,.15,.20\} , at 4–21 pp of coverage cost: the under-confident channel cannot separate correct items from hallucinations, so the threshold mostly removes correct items. We recommend that audits of LLM recommenders report calibration alongside OOD, and use catalog-anchored elicitation rather than generic confidence prompts. Keywords: Large Language Models, Recommender Systems, Hallucination, Confidence Calibration, Catalog Faithfulness, Selective Prediction 1. Introduction LLM-based recommenders are now in production for top- K K item suggestion across e-commerce, media, and local services ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Bao et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ) . They also routinely emit titles that do not exist in the target catalog. The dominant response in the literature is engineering-driven grounding: RecLM-cgen ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , logit-space constrained fine-tuning ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , bi-step grounding ( Bao et al., 2025 ) , and retrieval rewriting ( Shen et al., 2025 ) all aim to drive an out-of-domain rate, OOD@ K K , toward zero. The residual failures these systems still produce are reported as a single binary quantity. A grounded recommender that is equally confident on its surviving hallucinations as on its correct items is indistinguishable from a calibrated one to any policy that gates on confidence. Recent calls for holistic generative-recommender evaluation flag exactly this gap ( Deldjoo et al., 2025 ) . Whether the model knew it was hallucinating is, empirically, a question about the joint distribution of the catalog-membership indicator and the model’s verbalized confidence. We use “know” operationally throughout, referring to the model’s verbalized confidence channel, without committing to a metaphysics of LLM knowledge. Two adjacent literatures have probed pieces of this joint distribution but not the joint itself. LLM-calibration work measures expected calibration error, Brier score, and reliability against open-ended QA oracles ( Tian et al., 2023 ; Xiong et al., 2024 ; Kadavath et al., 2022 ; Geng et al., 2024 ) . Recent theory connects miscalibration to hallucination as a population-level phenomenon ( Kalai and Vempala, 2024 ; Kalai et al., 2025 ) . The closest neighbor in recommendation, Kweon et al. ( Kweon et al., 2025 ) , decomposes uncertainty against ranking correctness . To our knowledge, no prior work reports probabilistic calibration metrics jointly with catalog-faithfulness rate for LLM recommenders. This paper makes three contributions. First, a joint-audit protocol for catalog-faithful LLM recommenders combining OOD@ K K , popularity-stratified calibration (ECE, Brier, reliability), and a split-conformal abstention threshold with a finite-sample marginal score-quantile guarantee ( Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ; Kamath et al., 2020 ; Wen et al., 2025 ) . We operationalize the protocol on three catalogs of contrasting size and canonicity—MovieLens-25M (62K titles), Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys & Games (890K items), Yelp Open Dataset (150K regional businesses)—and four instruction-tuned LLMs from four independent vendors (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6). Second, a diagnostic finding that the binding constraint on inference-time abstention is the calibration quality of the verbalized-confidence channel, not the conformal procedure: LLMs are systematically under -confident on catalog-faithfulness, hedging on correct and hallucinated items alike. Third, an empirical ceiling on verbalized-confidence-driven abstention: across our α \alpha sweep, hallucination reduction tops out at 0.7 pp at 4–21 pp coverage cost. Together the three contributions argue that audits of LLM recommenders should report calibration alongside OOD as separate axes of model quality. 2. Related Work LLM-recommender hallucination. A growing line of work targets out-of-catalog generation in LLM recommenders. RecLM ( Liu et al., 2025a ) unifies three grounding strategies; LCFT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) constrains logits to the catalog at fine-tuning time; bi-step grounding ( Bao et al., 2025 ) retrieves candidates before generating; the Alipay search system ( Shen et al., 2025 ) rewrites generative retrieval queries to suppress hallucination at scale; ETEGRec ( Liu et al., 2025b ) learns end-to-end item tokens; and TIGER ( Rajput et al., 2023 ) encodes items via semantic IDs. Across these systems, the dominant evaluation protocol reports a binary in-catalog rate, not a faithfulness distribution conditioned on confidence. Holistic-evaluation proposals ( Deldjoo et al., 2025 ) argue this protocol is too coarse for generative recommenders, but do not themselves report calibration. LLM calibration, selective prediction, and abstention. The calibration literature elicits confidence by token logprobs ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) , verbalized self-assessment ( Tian et al., 2023 ) , or structured prompting ( Xiong et al., 2024 ; Geng et al., 2024 ) . Semantic entropy ( Farquhar et al., 2024 ) provides a generation-internal hallucination signal. Selective prediction and abstention give bounded-error guarantees under shift ( Kamath et al., 2020 ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , with AbstentionBench ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) documenting that reasoning fine-tuning can degrade abstention by up to 24%. None of this work has been applied to recommendation catalog faithfulness. Closest neighbor. Closest in spirit, Kweon et al. ( Kweon et al., 2025 ) quantify and decompose epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty for LLM recommenders on MovieLens-1M, Amazon-Grocery, and Steam. Their oracle is ranking correctness ; ours is catalog membership . A model can correlate uncertainty with NDCG-style ranking quality while shipping titles that do not exist in the catalog at all—the two oracles answer different operational questions, and the calibration that matters for serving end-users is the existence-of-item one. Beyond the oracle distinction, we additionally measure hallucination rate (OOD@ K K ) jointly with confidence and propose an inference-time conformal abstention threshold with a finite-sample marginal score-quantile guarantee ( Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ) . 3. Methodology 3.1. Datasets and catalog construction We audit three catalogs spanning canonical entertainment, long-tail e-commerce, and regional services. MovieLens-25M ( Harper and Konstan, 2015 ) contributes 62,423 movies with rich title and year metadata that recurs heavily in LLM pre-training data. Amazon Reviews 2023 Toys & Games ( Hou et al., 2024 ) contributes 890,874 product titles, the large majority of which are obscure long-tail items. Yelp Open Dataset ( Yelp, 2024 ) contributes 150,346 businesses keyed by name and city, with strong regional concentration. For each catalog we construct an audit set of 300 users with at least 30 prior interactions, plus a disjoint held-out set of 100 users for conformal calibration; per-cell audit counts are 285–300 users after dropping errored or unparseable responses (only GPT-OSS on Amazon and Yelp falls below 300). Items are stratified into popularity quartiles by interaction count; we report head (Q1) and long-tail (Q4) statistics in Section 4 . 3.2. LLMs and prompting protocol We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs from four independent vendors: Mistral Large (via La Plateforme), Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-120B (both via Together AI), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic). Each receives a zero-shot prompt containing the user’s 30 most recent interactions and produces a top-10 list. Decoding is held fixed across models (temperature 0, K = 10 K=10 , a single fixed system prompt); the full prompt templates are in Appendix A . 3.3. Hallucination measurement For each generated title we test exact match against the catalog; on miss, we apply normalized fuzzy matching ( token_set_ratio ≥ 90 \geq 90 on lowercased, punctuation-stripped strings) to absorb formatting variants. Items failing both tests are coded as out-of-domain. We report OOD@10 aggregate and per-quartile rates. 3.4. Confidence elicitation We use verbalized self-rated confidence on a 0–100 scale, elicited via the Tian et al. ( Tian et al., 2023 ) “Just Ask” template, applied uniformly across all LLMs. Verbalized confidence is the natural elicitation for production deployment: it works uniformly across closed-source APIs and open-weight models, and Tian et al. document that token logprobs on RLHF’d LLMs are systematically over-confident relative to verbalized self-rating—verbalized confidence often outperforms logprobs as a calibration signal on instruction-tuned models. Cross-vendor replication across the LLMs in our audit serves as the cross-channel robustness control. We do not assume calibration quality is uniform across model families; that is precisely the audit’s empirical question. We additionally run a prompt-perturbation ablation on Llama-3.3-70B × \times Yelp, replacing “Just Ask” with a prompt that explicitly anchors confidence to catalog membership (results in Section 6 ). 3.5. Calibration metrics and conformal threshold We report Expected Calibration Error (ECE) using 10-bin equal-width binning over normalized verbalized confidence. We report Brier score alongside ECE; Brier is binning-free and serves as a robustness check against equal-width-bin artifacts. Reliability diagrams (Figure 1 ) are drawn per cell and stratified by Q1 head and Q4 tail. For the conformal threshold we follow split-conformal calibration ( Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024 ) . Let c i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c_{i}\in[0,1] denote normalized verbalized confidence on calibration item i i , and define the nonconformity score s i = 1 − c i s_{i}=1-c_{i} . Let q ^ α \hat{q}_{\alpha} be the ⌈ ( n + 1 ) ​ ( 1 − α ) ⌉ / n \lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil/n empirical quantile of { s i } i = 1 n \{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} over in-catalog calibration items. Under exchangeability of calibration and test items, split-conformal yields marginal coverage on the score quantile, Pr [ s test ≤ q ^ α ] ≥ 1 − α \Pr[s_{\text{test}}\leq\hat{q}_{\alpha}]\geq 1-\alpha , retaining roughly a 1 − α 1-\alpha fraction of new items. This is not a guarantee on hallucination rate: transferring it to Pr ⁡ [ hallucination at ​ q ^ α ] ≤ α \Pr[\text{hallucination at }\hat{q}_{\alpha}]\leq\alpha requires s i s_{i} to be a calibrated indicator of hallucination probability, which Section 4 shows fails for verbalized confidence on the LLMs we audit. The guarantee is also marginal : subgroup hallucination rates—in particular long-tail strata—may exceed any chosen rate even when score-quantile coverage holds. We therefore report empirical retained-set hallucination rates in Section 5 and let the data, rather than the bound, carry the operational story. 4. Findings We present three findings, anchored in Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 1 . Table 1. OOD@10 hallucination rate (mean over audit users; 95% paired-user bootstrap CI in brackets). Hallucination is catalog-dependent OOD@10 in Table 1 traces a monotone gradient by catalog canonicity : near-zero on MovieLens (0–0.2%), 4.5–8.3% on Amazon Toys, 2.2–8.4% on Yelp. Our hypothesis is memorization at pre-training scale—MovieLens titles are canonical English-language film entries seen thousands of times in any web-scale corpus, Amazon Toys are long-tail product strings rarely surfaced outside Amazon’s retail pages, and Yelp couples business names to U.S. cities with strong regional concentration. At frontier-LLM scale, the model reproduces what it has memorized at pre-training time and confabulates the rest. Two observations support the memorization story over a model-scale story. The gradient does not track parameter count: GPT-OSS-120B—the largest model in our lineup—is the worst offender on both long-tail catalogs, and Mistral, Llama, and Claude form a joint-best cluster on Amazon (overlapping bootstrap CIs in Table 1 ) with GPT-OSS distinguishably worse. On Yelp the joint-best set narrows to Mistral and Llama (Llama [.017,.028], Mistral [.023,.041]); Claude’s CI [.033,.049] does not overlap Llama’s, suggestive of a training-mixture gap in regional-business coverage rather than raw capacity. The operational consequence is direct: representation-level grounding (RecLM ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , LCFT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ) is most valuable on the long-tail end of the canonicity gradient; on canonical catalogs at frontier scale, OOD@10 is already near zero and the binding evaluation axis is calibration, not catalog faithfulness. 4.2. LLMs are systematically under-confident on catalog faithfulness The headline calibration finding is in Table 2 and Figure 1 . On MovieLens, where OOD@10 is effectively zero, head-stratum ECE is 0.138 for Mistral, 0.203 for Llama, 0.166 for GPT-OSS, and 0.223 for Claude—a 14–22 percentage-point gap between verbalized confidence and empirical accuracy. The direction is consistent across all twelve cells: LLMs verbalize a mean confidence of 67–86 even when their actual catalog-hit rate is 92–100%. Reliability curves in Figure 1 sit above the perfect-calibration diagonal in every panel and for every LLM. The pattern is therefore one of under-confidence , not the over-confidence usually emphasized in the LLM-hallucination literature. Tian et al. ( Tian et al., 2023 ) and Xiong et al. ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) report mostly over-confidence on QA-style tasks; the catalog-faithfulness regime tested here flips the direction, and the flip replicates across all four independently trained vendor families—Claude is the most aggressively under-confident, verbalizing as low as 45 on items recommended with ≥ \geq 95% accuracy on Yelp. Brier scores corroborate the binning result, with Mistral lowest in all six (dataset, stratum) cells of Table 2 (0.020–0.041) and Claude highest (0.052–0.128). Why does verbalized confidence sit so far below catalog-hit rate? “Just Ask” elicits a generic recommendation-quality rating, not a catalog-membership probability; LLMs have no separate mechanism to introspect catalog membership and instead rate taste in the hedged 67–86 band trained in by RLHF, while existence accuracy on the catalogs we test is 92–100%. Two catalog-anchored prompt-perturbation ablations support this reading by moving the channel in opposite directions on the same task: on Llama × \times Yelp the perturbed prompt drops ECE 0.224 → \to 0.141 and reshapes confidence bimodally (82% at 100, 14% at 0); on Claude × \times Yelp the same prompt instead lowers mean confidence by 14 points (67 → \to 53) while accuracy stays at 96%, widening the reliability gap and raising ECE to 0.434. Both shifts—in opposite directions—confirm that prompt phrasing materially moves the verbalized channel while catalog-hit rate is essentially constant; under-confidence is an elicitation mismatch as much as a calibration gap, and its magnitude and form are template- and vendor-specific. The practical implication is the inverse of the typical concern: a downstream policy that gates on verbalized confidence conservatively rejects items the model has correct, leaving accuracy on the table rather than letting hallucinations through. On Yelp, ECE-tail exceeds ECE-head for every LLM (Mistral 0.180 → \to 0.191, Llama 0.242 → \to 0.280, GPT-OSS 0.191 → \to 0.229, Claude 0.323 → \to 0.350). Discussion and Limitations Four LLMs and three catalogs are a deliberate cross-section, not a comprehensive sweep. The subjects are zero-shot frontier LLMs used directly as recommenders; grounded, fine-tuned, and retrieval-constrained stacks are the more common production configuration and may hallucinate and calibrate differently, so the results characterize the zero-shot regime rather than deployed grounded systems. Public benchmark catalogs may also not reflect production catalog churn, regional inventory drift, or temporal staleness. Verbalized confidence is one elicitation among many and interacts with prompt phrasing ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) : the two catalog-anchored ablations of § 4 move the channel in opposite directions on the same task (on Llama the catalog-anchored prompt also cuts OOD@10 from 2.2% to 0.3%, acting like in-prompt retrieval, while on Claude it deepens under-confidence), so verbalized confidence is not a uniform abstention signal across vendors. Logprob aggregates ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) and semantic entropy ( Farquhar et al., 2024 ) are the alternatives where cross-LLM consistency is required, but token logprobs are exposed by only some providers. A logprob check on Llama × \times Yelp ( n = 3,000 n{=}3{,}000 ) is also under-confident (ECE 0.182 vs 0.213 verbalized), so the effect is not merely a verbalization artifact. The conformal guarantee is on the score quantile and marginal across items; long-tail-stratum hallucination rates may rise above any chosen α \alpha even when score-quantile coverage holds. Exchangeability between calibration and test items underwrites it and fails under temporal or popularity drift, so deployment needs periodic re-calibration. Representation-level fixes such as RecLM ( Liu et al., 2025a ) and LCFT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) are complementary, and the natural next step is to compose conformal abstention with grounded generation; reasoning fine-tuning can itself degrade abstention by up to 24% ( Kirichenko et al., 2025 ) . Our recommendation that audits report calibration alongside OOD therefore applies to the zero-shot verbalized-confidence regime; calibrating grounded recommenders is the necessary follow-up this work does not address. Appendix A Prompt templates This appendix gives the exact prompt templates referenced in the paper’s Methodology section. Two templates were used: a base verbalized-confidence template for all main results, and a catalog-anchored perturbation template for the ablation in Section 4.2. The membership, catalog, and popularity variants that exist in the released code are exploratory and are not part of the results reported in the paper. Appendix B Decoding and prompting configuration All four evaluated LLMs (Mistral Large, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6) received identical decoding and prompting settings: temperature 0, top- K = 10 K=10 , the user’s interaction history truncated to its 30 most recent items, no few-shot examples, and a single fixed system prompt held constant across models. In each template below, {history} is the numbered list of the user’s recent item titles in chronological order (most recent last), and {k} is set to 10. Model responses were parsed with a tolerant line-level regular expression extracting (rank, title, confidence) triples. Appendix C Template 1: base verbalized-confidence prompt (“Just Ask”) Used for all main results: out-of-domain (OOD@10) hallucination rates, calibration metrics (ECE, Brier), reliability diagrams, and the split-conformal abstention sweep. The verbalized-confidence question follows the “Just Ask” format of Tian et al. (2023). System prompt: You are a recommender system. Given a user’s interaction history, recommend items they might enjoy next, along with your confidence (0-100) for each recommendation. User prompt: User’s interaction history (chronological order, most recent last): {history} Provide your top {k} next-item recommendations along with your confidence (0-100) that each is a good recommendation. Output ONLY the recommendations in this exact format, one per line: 1. <item title> | <confidence> 2. <item title> | <confidence> ... {k}. <item title> | <confidence> Do not output any preamble, explanations, or commentary. Appendix D Template 2: catalog-anchored perturbation prompt Used for the prompt-perturbation ablation in Section 4.2, applied to Llama-3.3-70B and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Yelp. This variant anchors the confidence question to catalog membership (the quantity OOD@10 measures) rather than to generic recommendation quality, while holding the output format fixed. System prompt: You are a recommender system that recommends items from a fixed catalog. Given a user’s interaction history (each entry is an item from the catalog), recommend items from the same catalog they might enjoy next. User prompt: User’s interaction history (chronological order, most recent last): {history} Provide your top {k} next-item recommendations from the catalog. For each recommendation, give your confidence (0-100) that the title you wrote is an actual entry in the catalog (i.e., the item exists with that exact name in the dataset; not invented, hallucinated, or paraphrased). Output ONLY the recommendations in this exact format, one per line: 1. <item title> | <confidence> 2. <item title> | <confidence> ... {k}. <item title> | <confidence> Do not output any preamble, explanations, or commentary.
